Feature Hierarchy

ImageNet's ResNet-18, unchanged, on a few of the notebook's flower photos. At the top, its 64 first-layer filters. Below, for each stage of the network, the eight channels that respond most strongly to the chosen photo: early stages fire on edges and colors at full detail, late stages on large parts of the flower at coarse resolution. Click a map to lay it over the photo.

The map you clicked

conv1: 64 filters of 7 × 7 × 3, learned on ImageNet

Each filter is shown as a tiny color image, scaled to its own range. Oriented edges and stripes, color blobs and color edges: the same kinds of detectors as Sobel kernels and color filters, learned rather than designed.

The eight most active channels at each stage

getting these maps in PyTorch 

    

  






  

    
Detail goes down, meaning goes up
Each stage halves the resolution (112, 56, 28, 14, 7) and widens what one value sees. conv1's maps still look like the photo; layer4's 7 × 7 maps only say roughly where on the photo a large pattern was found.

    
Why the early layers transfer
None of the early maps depends on which 1,000 classes ImageNet happened to have: edges and colors are needed for any photo. That is why feature extraction keeps them frozen and fine-tuning changes them last, if at all.

    
Most active is not most important
Ranking channels by their mean response is a simple way to choose eight of hundreds. A channel can matter for the decision while staying weak on average; this page shows what fires, not why the network decides.
